title: What R and CRAN are
text: R is a free language and environment for statistics and graphics. CRAN, the Comprehensive R Archive Network, is where you download R itself and most add-on packages. You type commands at the console prompt, or save them in a script so the same steps can be run again later.
keywords: R language CRAN download install R statistics software
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: RStudio Desktop and the RStudio IDE
text: RStudio is a free editor (IDE) that runs on top of R. It shows your script, the console, the environment of saved objects and your plots in one window. R must be installed first; RStudio then finds it and uses it.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: RStudio IDE User Guide â RStudio User Guide

title: Posit Cloud
text: Posit Cloud runs RStudio in a web browser, so you can do the course work without installing R on your laptop. Each project lives in the cloud; packages you install belong to that project, so a new project may need them installed again.
keywords: Posit Cloud browser online RStudio cloud
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Assigning values with <-
text: Use <- to store a value under a name, for example x <- 5. The name then refers to that value until you assign something else. = also works at the top level, but <- is the usual R style. Names are case sensitive, so Total and total are different objects.
keywords: assignment assign variable store value arrow
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Vectors and c()
text: A vector is R's basic data structure: an ordered set of values of one type. c() combines values into a vector, for example ages <- c(19, 22, 31). Most R functions work on a whole vector at once, so you rarely need a loop for simple arithmetic.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: R: Combine Values into a Vector or List

title: Sequences: :, seq() and rep()
text: 1:10 makes the whole numbers from 1 to 10. seq() gives more control, for example seq(0, 1, by = 0.25) or seq(1, 100, length.out = 5). rep() repeats values, for example rep("a", 3) or rep(c(1, 2), times = 2).
keywords: sequence seq rep repeat numbers range
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Basic data types
text: The common atomic types are numeric (double), integer, character (text in quotes), and logical (TRUE or FALSE). class() and typeof() tell you what you have. Mixing types in c() coerces everything to the most flexible type, so c(1, "a") becomes character.
keywords: data types numeric character logical integer class typeof type
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Vector arithmetic and recycling
text: Arithmetic operators such as + - * / ^ work element by element on vectors. If one vector is shorter, R recycles it to match the longer one, so c(1, 2, 3, 4) * 2 doubles every value. R warns when the longer length is not a multiple of the shorter one.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Getting help in R
text: Type ?mean or help(mean) to open the help page for a function, and help.search("regression") or ??regression to search all installed help pages. Each help page lists the arguments, their defaults, what the function returns and runnable examples at the bottom.
keywords: help documentation question mark help page
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Installing and loading packages
text: install.packages("dplyr") downloads a package from CRAN once per computer (or per Posit Cloud project). library(dplyr) loads it, and you must do that in every new R session. The error "there is no package called" means the package is not installed yet; "could not find function" often means it is installed but not loaded.
keywords: install packages install.packages package library error no package called
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: R: Install Packages from Repositories or Local Files

title: library() and the search path
text: library(pkg) attaches an installed package so its functions can be called by name. You can also call one function without attaching, with pkg::fun(), for example dplyr::filter(). search() shows which packages are currently attached.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: R: Loading/Attaching and Listing of Packages

title: Working directory and file paths
text: getwd() shows the folder R reads files from and setwd() changes it. A relative path like "data/sales.csv" is looked up from the working directory, which is why a file can be found in one session and not in another. RStudio projects set the working directory to the project folder for you.
keywords: working directory path folder file location getwd setwd
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: R: Get or Set Working Directory

title: Scripts, comments and running code
text: Comments start with # and R ignores the rest of the line, so use them to explain why a step is there. Keep your work in a script file and run it from the top so results can be reproduced. source("file.R") runs a whole script from the console.
keywords: script comment source run code reproducible
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: R: Read R Code from a File, a Connection or Expressions

title: What a data frame is
syllabus_topic: Lecture 2: Using R to manipulate data (data frames)
text: A data frame is a table: each column is a vector of one type and all columns have the same length. data.frame(name = c("A", "B"), score = c(80, 92)) builds one by hand. Most data you read from files arrives as a data frame.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Looking at a data frame: str(), head(), summary()
syllabus_topic: Lecture 2: Using R to manipulate data (data frames)
text: str(df) shows each column's type and first values, head(df) shows the first 6 rows (tail() the last 6), and summary(df) gives a quick summary for every column. nrow(), ncol() and dim() report the size. Run these first whenever you load new data.
keywords: inspect explore structure str head summary dataset
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: R: Compactly Display the Structure of an Arbitrary R Object

title: head() and tail()
syllabus_topic: Lecture 2: Using R to manipulate data (data frames)
text: head(x, n) returns the first n rows of a data frame or the first n values of a vector; tail(x, n) returns the last n. The default n is 6. A negative n drops that many from the other end.
keywords: first rows last rows head tail
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: R: Return the First or Last Parts of an Object

title: nrow(), ncol() and dim()
syllabus_topic: Lecture 2: Using R to manipulate data (data frames)
text: nrow(df) gives the number of rows and ncol(df) the number of columns; dim(df) returns both. length() of a data frame gives the number of columns, not rows, which surprises many beginners.
keywords: number of rows columns size dimensions nrow ncol dim
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: R: The Number of Rows/Columns of an Array

title: Selecting columns with $ and [[ ]]
syllabus_topic: Lecture 2: Using R to manipulate data (data frames)
text: df$score returns the score column as a vector. df[["score"]] does the same and also works when the column name is stored in a variable. A misspelled name after $ returns NULL rather than an error, so check names(df) if a column seems empty.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: R: Extract or Replace Parts of an Object

title: Indexing rows and columns with [ , ]
syllabus_topic: Lecture 2: Using R to manipulate data (data frames)
text: df[rows, columns] picks parts of a data frame. df[1:3, ] gives the first three rows and all columns; df[, c("name", "score")] gives two columns; negative numbers drop positions, so df[-1, ] removes the first row. Leaving a side blank means take everything.
keywords: index indexing rows columns brackets square brackets subset
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: R: Extract or Replace Parts of a Data Frame

title: Subsetting with logical conditions
syllabus_topic: Lecture 2: Using R to manipulate data (data frames)
text: A comparison such as df$score > 80 gives a TRUE or FALSE for each row, and df[df$score > 80, ] keeps the TRUE rows. Combine conditions with & (and) and | (or). Use == to compare, because a single = is assignment.
keywords: filter rows condition logical comparison subset base R
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: which() and %in%
syllabus_topic: Lecture 2: Using R to manipulate data (data frames)
text: which(x > 10) returns the positions where a logical vector is TRUE, ignoring NA. x %in% c("a", "b") checks membership for every value and returns TRUE or FALSE, which is handy for filtering rows to a set of categories.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: subset()
syllabus_topic: Lecture 2: Using R to manipulate data (data frames)
text: subset(df, score > 80, select = c(name, score)) is base R's readable way to filter rows and pick columns in one call. Rows where the condition is NA are dropped. It is convenient at the console; in functions, [ ] indexing is safer.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: R: Subsetting Vectors, Matrices and Data Frames

title: Sorting with order() and sort()
syllabus_topic: Lecture 2: Using R to manipulate data (data frames)
text: sort(x) returns a sorted vector. To sort a data frame, use order(): df[order(df$score), ] sorts rows by score, and df[order(-df$score), ] or order(df$score, decreasing = TRUE) sorts high to low.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Adding and changing columns
syllabus_topic: Lecture 2: Using R to manipulate data (data frames)
text: Assigning to a new name creates a column: df$pct <- df$score / 100. Assigning to an existing name replaces it, and df$pct <- NULL removes it. The new vector must have one value per row (or one value that is recycled).
keywords: add column new column change column remove column
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: R: Extract or Replace Parts of a Data Frame

title: Lists
syllabus_topic: Lecture 2: Using R to manipulate data (data frames)
text: A list holds elements of different types and lengths, for example list(name = "A", scores = c(1, 2, 3)). Use [[ ]] or $ to get one element out and [ ] to get a smaller list. A data frame is a special list whose elements are equal-length columns, and JSON data often arrives as nested lists.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: R: Lists - Generic and Dotted Pairs

title: Factors for categories
syllabus_topic: Lecture 2: Using R to manipulate data (data frames)
text: A factor stores categorical data with a fixed set of levels, for example factor(c("low", "high", "low")). levels() lists the categories and table() counts them. summary() of a factor gives counts per level, not a mean. To turn a numeric-looking factor into numbers, use as.numeric(as.character(f)).
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Missing values: NA and is.na()
syllabus_topic: Lecture 2: Using R to manipulate data (data frames)
text: NA marks a missing value. Most calculations with NA return NA, and NA == NA is NA, so test with is.na(x) instead. sum(is.na(x)) counts the missing values and complete.cases(df) flags rows with nothing missing.
keywords: missing values NA is.na missing data
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: dplyr filter(): keep rows
syllabus_topic: Lecture 2: Using R to manipulate data (data frames)
text: filter(df, score > 80, year == 2024) keeps the rows where every condition is TRUE; separate conditions with commas mean "and". Rows where a condition is NA are dropped. Load dplyr with library(dplyr) first.
keywords: filter rows dplyr subset keep rows condition
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: Keep or drop rows that match a condition | filter • dplyr

title: dplyr select(): pick columns
syllabus_topic: Lecture 2: Using R to manipulate data (data frames)
text: select(df, name, score) keeps those columns, select(df, -id) drops one, and helpers such as starts_with("q") pick columns by name pattern. select() never changes the rows.
keywords: select columns dplyr choose columns drop columns
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: Keep or drop columns using their names and types | select • dplyr

title: dplyr mutate(): create or change columns
syllabus_topic: Lecture 2: Using R to manipulate data (data frames)
text: mutate(df, pct = score / 100) adds a column computed from existing ones; using an existing name overwrites that column. Columns created earlier in the same mutate() call can be used later in it.
keywords: mutate new column create column calculate dplyr
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: Create, modify, and delete columns | mutate • dplyr

title: dplyr arrange(): sort rows
syllabus_topic: Lecture 2: Using R to manipulate data (data frames)
text: arrange(df, score) sorts rows from low to high and arrange(df, desc(score)) from high to low. Give several columns to break ties. Missing values are always placed at the end.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: Order rows using column values | arrange • dplyr

title: group_by() and summarise()
syllabus_topic: Lecture 2: Using R to manipulate data (data frames)
text: group_by(df, region) marks groups, and summarise() then returns one row per group, for example summarise(n = n(), avg = mean(sales, na.rm = TRUE)). Without group_by(), summarise() returns a single row for the whole table.
keywords: group by summarise summarize aggregate group means groups
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: Summarise each group down to one row | summarise • dplyr

title: count() for quick frequency tables
syllabus_topic: Lecture 2: Using R to manipulate data (data frames)
text: count(df, region) returns each value with how many rows have it, and count(df, region, sort = TRUE) puts the most common first. It is a shortcut for group_by() followed by summarise(n = n()).
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: Count the observations in each group | count • dplyr

title: Joining tables
syllabus_topic: Lecture 2: Using R to manipulate data (data frames)
text: left_join(x, y, by = "id") keeps every row of x and adds matching columns from y (NA where there is no match). inner_join() keeps only rows that match in both. Check the row count after a join: duplicate keys in y create extra rows.
keywords: join merge combine tables left join inner join
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: The pipe %>%
syllabus_topic: Lecture 2: Using R to manipulate data (data frames)
text: x %>% f(y) means f(x, y), so steps read left to right: df %>% filter(score > 80) %>% arrange(score). %>% comes from magrittr and is re-exported by dplyr, so you need library(dplyr) or library(magrittr) in the session, or R reports could not find function "%>%".
keywords: pipe magrittr %>% could not find function %>%
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: The native pipe |>
syllabus_topic: Lecture 2: Using R to manipulate data (data frames)
text: Since R 4.1.0, base R has its own pipe, |>, which needs no package: df |> head(). The right-hand side must be a function call with parentheses. It behaves like %>% for most everyday code.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: pivot_longer(): wide to long
syllabus_topic: Lecture 2: Using R to manipulate data (data frames)
text: pivot_longer(df, cols = c(q1, q2, q3), names_to = "quarter", values_to = "sales") turns several columns into two: one holding the old column names and one holding the values. Long data is what ggplot2 and group_by() work with best.
keywords: pivot longer reshape wide to long tidyr
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: Pivot data from wide to long | pivot_longer • tidyr

title: drop_na(): remove rows with missing values
syllabus_topic: Lecture 2: Using R to manipulate data (data frames)
text: drop_na(df) removes every row that has a missing value in any column, and drop_na(df, score) only looks at the score column. Check how many rows you lose, because dropping too much can bias results.
keywords: drop missing rows remove NA drop_na
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: Drop rows containing missing values | drop_na • tidyr

title: mean() and na.rm
text: mean(x) returns the average. If x contains any NA the result is NA, unless you write mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), which removes missing values first. The trim argument gives a trimmed mean that ignores extreme values.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: median()
text: median(x) returns the middle value, or the average of the two middle values when there is an even number. It is less affected by extreme values than the mean. Like mean(), it needs na.rm = TRUE when there are missing values.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Standard deviation and variance
text: sd(x) gives the standard deviation and var(x) the variance; both use n - 1 in the denominator (the sample versions). Both accept na.rm = TRUE. The standard deviation is in the same units as the data, which makes it easier to read.
keywords: standard deviation variance spread sd var
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: range(), min() and max()
text: min(x) and max(x) return the smallest and largest values; range(x) returns both as a vector of two. All three accept na.rm = TRUE. which.min() and which.max() tell you the position of the extreme value.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: quantile()
text: quantile(x) returns the minimum, 25th percentile, median, 75th percentile and maximum. quantile(x, probs = c(0.1, 0.9)) asks for other cut points. Set na.rm = TRUE if values are missing; otherwise quantile() stops with an error.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: summary()
text: summary() of a numeric vector shows the minimum, quartiles, median, mean, maximum and the count of NAs. Applied to a data frame it does this for every column, and for factors it shows counts per level. For an lm model it prints the regression table.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: table() for counts
text: table(x) counts how often each value appears; table(x, y) builds a two-way cross-tabulation. prop.table(table(x)) turns counts into proportions. By default NA is not counted; useNA = "ifany" adds it.
keywords: table counts frequency crosstab cross tabulation
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: R: Cross Tabulation and Table Creation

title: Histograms with hist()
text: hist(x) draws a histogram, splitting the values into bins and showing how many fall in each. The breaks argument changes the number or position of bins. Use it to see the shape of a distribution: symmetric, skewed or with outliers.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Correlation with cor()
text: cor(x, y) gives the Pearson correlation, from -1 to 1, which measures how closely two numeric variables follow a straight line. With missing values add use = "complete.obs". Correlation is not causation.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Writing your own function
text: Define a function with function(): square <- function(x) { x^2 }. Arguments can have defaults, for example function(x, na.rm = TRUE). The value of the last expression is returned, or you can use return() to leave early.
keywords: write function create function define function custom function arguments return
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: if and else
text: if (condition) { ... } else { ... } runs one branch. The condition must be a single TRUE or FALSE; a vector or NA gives an error. For element-by-element choices on a whole vector, use ifelse(test, yes, no) instead.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: ifelse() for vectors
text: ifelse(score >= 50, "pass", "fail") returns a vector the same length as score, choosing yes or no element by element. It is the vectorised partner of if/else and works well inside mutate().
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: for loops
text: for (i in 1:10) { ... } runs the body once for each value. seq_along(x) is safer than 1:length(x) because it gives an empty sequence when x is empty. If you build a result inside a loop, create the vector first and fill it in.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: apply(), sapply() and lapply()
text: lapply(x, f) applies f to each element and returns a list; sapply() does the same but simplifies the result to a vector when it can. apply(m, 1, f) works across the rows of a matrix (2 for columns). They often replace a loop.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: R: Apply a Function over a List or Vector

title: tapply() for group summaries
text: tapply(values, groups, mean) applies a function to the values within each group, for example average sales per region. It is a base R alternative to group_by() plus summarise().
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: R: Apply a Function Over a Ragged Array

title: Random samples with sample()
text: sample(x, size) draws size values from x without replacement; add replace = TRUE to sample with replacement, as in bootstrapping. sample(nrow(df), 10) gives 10 random row numbers you can use to sample rows.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: set.seed() for reproducible randomness
text: Random numbers in R come from a generator. set.seed(42) before sample() or rnorm() makes the same random results every time, so others can reproduce your work. Change or remove the seed to get new draws.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: replicate() to repeat a simulation
text: replicate(1000, mean(sample(x, 30))) repeats an expression many times and collects the results. It is a quick way to build a sampling distribution, for example of the sample mean.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: R: Apply a Function over a List or Vector

title: Sampling distributions and the central limit idea
text: If you take many random samples and compute each sample's mean, those means vary less than the raw data and, for reasonably large samples, form a roughly normal shape around the population mean. Their spread shrinks as the sample size grows. You can see this in R with replicate() and hist().
keywords: sampling distribution central limit theorem sample mean
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Normal distribution functions
text: rnorm(n, mean, sd) generates random normal values; dnorm() gives the density, pnorm() the probability of being below a value, and qnorm() the value for a given probability. The same d, p, q, r pattern exists for other distributions such as runif() and rbinom().
keywords: normal distribution rnorm pnorm qnorm random numbers
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: t.test() for comparing means
text: t.test(x, mu = 50) tests whether a mean differs from 50; t.test(score ~ group, data = df) compares two group means. The output gives the t statistic, a p-value and a 95 percent confidence interval. A small p-value suggests a difference unlikely to be due to chance alone.
keywords: t test hypothesis test p-value confidence interval compare means inferential
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Reading CSV files with read.csv()
syllabus_topic: Lecture 5: Connecting with external data sources (JSON)
text: read.csv("file.csv") reads a comma separated file into a data frame. The first row is used as column names (header = TRUE). Text that should be numeric but contains symbols like $ or , will be read as character, so check with str().
keywords: read csv import file load data
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: readr read_csv()
syllabus_topic: Lecture 5: Connecting with external data sources (JSON)
text: readr's read_csv("file.csv") is a faster tidyverse reader that returns a tibble and prints the column types it guessed. Use col_types to set types yourself. It can also read straight from a URL.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: Read a delimited file (including CSV and TSV) into a tibble | read_delim • readr

title: Writing data with write.csv()
syllabus_topic: Lecture 5: Connecting with external data sources (JSON)
text: write.csv(df, "out.csv", row.names = FALSE) saves a data frame as a CSV file. Without row.names = FALSE, R adds an extra unnamed column of row numbers.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: "cannot open file" errors
syllabus_topic: Lecture 5: Connecting with external data sources (JSON)
text: "cannot open file ... No such file or directory" means R looked for the file in the wrong place or the name is misspelled. Check getwd(), list.files() and the exact path, including the file extension.

written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Reading JSON with jsonlite::fromJSON()
syllabus_topic: Lecture 5: Connecting with external data sources (JSON)
text: fromJSON() from the jsonlite package converts JSON text, a file or a URL into R objects. By default it simplifies arrays of records into a data frame. toJSON() goes the other way.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Nested JSON and flatten
syllabus_topic: Lecture 5: Connecting with external data sources (JSON)
text: JSON records can contain nested objects, which arrive as data frames inside a column. fromJSON(x, flatten = TRUE) or jsonlite::flatten(df) spreads them into ordinary columns with names like address.city.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Getting data from a web API
syllabus_topic: Lecture 5: Connecting with external data sources (JSON)
text: Many web APIs return JSON. You can pass the URL straight to fromJSON(), then inspect the result with str() to find the part you need, often a data frame inside a list. Check the API's documentation for paging and rate limits.
keywords: api web api url download json
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: Fetching JSON data from REST APIs

title: Converting text to numbers
syllabus_topic: Lecture 5: Connecting with external data sources (JSON)
text: as.numeric(x) converts text to numbers. Values that cannot be converted, such as "1,200" or "n/a", become NA with the warning "NAs introduced by coercion". Clean them first, for example with gsub(",", "", x).
keywords: convert text to numbers as.numeric coercion NAs introduced by coercion
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Text cleaning with gsub()
syllabus_topic: Lecture 5: Connecting with external data sources (JSON)
text: gsub(pattern, replacement, x) replaces every match of a pattern in each string; sub() replaces only the first. Use fixed = TRUE to treat the pattern as plain text rather than a regular expression.
keywords: replace text gsub sub string clean
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: paste() and paste0()
syllabus_topic: Lecture 5: Connecting with external data sources (JSON)
text: paste("a", "b") joins strings with a space and paste0("a", "b") joins them with nothing in between. Both are vectorised, so paste0("Q", 1:4) gives Q1 to Q4. collapse = ", " joins a vector into one string.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: ggplot() and layers
text: A ggplot2 chart starts with ggplot(data, aes(...)) and adds layers with +, for example ggplot(df, aes(x = height, y = weight)) + geom_point(). Nothing is drawn until at least one geom layer is added.
keywords: ggplot ggplot2 plot chart layers visualisation visualization
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: Create a new ggplot | ggplot • ggplot2

title: aes(): mapping versus setting
text: Inside aes(), you map a variable to an aesthetic, so colour = species gives each species its own colour and a legend. Outside aes(), you set a fixed value, so geom_point(colour = "blue") makes every point blue.
keywords: aes aesthetics colour color mapping fixed colour
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Scatter plots with geom_point()
text: geom_point() draws one point per row and shows the relationship between two numeric variables. Map size, shape or colour to extra variables, and set alpha to make overlapping points easier to read.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Line charts with geom_line()
text: geom_line() connects observations in order of the x variable, which suits time series. Use group = or colour = to draw one line per category.
keywords: line chart line graph time series geom_line
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Histograms with geom_histogram()
text: geom_histogram() shows the distribution of one numeric variable. ggplot2 uses 30 bins by default and tells you so; choose binwidth or bins yourself for a clearer picture.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: Histograms and frequency polygons | geom_freqpoly • ggplot2

title: Bar charts: geom_bar() and geom_col()
text: geom_bar() counts rows for each category itself. geom_col() uses heights you already have in the data, for example totals from summarise(). Use fill = to colour bars by a variable.
keywords: bar chart bar plot geom_bar geom_col
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Box plots with geom_boxplot()
text: geom_boxplot() shows the median, the middle 50 percent as a box, whiskers and outlying points for each group. It is a quick way to compare a numeric variable across categories.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: A box and whiskers plot (in the style of Tukey) | geom_boxplot • ggplot2

title: Titles and axis labels with labs()
text: labs(title = "...", x = "...", y = "...", colour = "...") sets the plot title, the axis labels and legend titles. Clear labels with units make a chart readable without extra explanation.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: Modify axis, legend, and plot labels | labs • ggplot2

title: Small multiples with facet_wrap()
text: facet_wrap(~ species) draws one panel per category with the same axes, which makes comparisons easy. ncol or nrow controls the layout and scales = "free" lets each panel have its own axis range.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: Wrap a 1d ribbon of panels into 2d | facet_wrap • ggplot2

title: "Aesthetics must be either length 1" errors
text: This ggplot2 error means a value given to an aesthetic has a different length from the data, often a whole vector from another data frame. Map columns of the same data frame inside aes(), or give a single fixed value outside aes().
keywords: aesthetics must be either length 1 error ggplot
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: map_data() for map outlines
text: ggplot2's map_data("state") turns a map from the maps package into a data frame with long, lat, group and region columns. Region names are lower case, so lower-case your own state names before joining.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: Create a data frame of map data | map_data • ggplot2

title: Drawing shapes with geom_polygon()
text: geom_polygon(aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group)) draws filled shapes such as states. group is essential: without it, separate shapes are joined by stray lines. Map fill = to a variable to make a choropleth.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Map projections with coord_map()
text: coord_map() projects longitude and latitude so maps do not look stretched; coord_quickmap() is a faster approximation. coord_map() needs the mapproj package installed.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: The maps package
text: The maps package contains outline data for the world, US states and US counties. It is what map_data() reads from, so install it with install.packages("maps") before using map_data().
keywords: maps package world map US states counties
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Adding points to a map
text: To show locations on a map, add a geom_point() layer with its own data, for example cities with longitude and latitude columns: + geom_point(data = cities, aes(x = lon, y = lat)). Each layer can use a different data frame.
keywords: points on map cities locations latitude longitude
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Fitting a linear model with lm()
text: lm(y ~ x, data = df) fits a straight line predicting y from x. Add predictors with +, as in lm(price ~ size + age, data = df). The ~ reads as "is modelled by". Save the model to an object so you can summarise and predict.
keywords: linear regression linear model lm fit model regression
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Reading summary() of an lm model
text: summary(model) shows each coefficient with its standard error, t value and p-value, plus R-squared. A coefficient is the expected change in y for a one-unit change in that predictor, holding the others fixed. R-squared is the share of variation in y explained by the model.
keywords: regression output coefficients r squared p value summary model
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: predict() with a linear model
text: predict(model, newdata = new_df) returns predictions for new rows. new_df must have columns with the same names as the predictors. interval = "confidence" or "prediction" adds lower and upper bounds.
keywords: predict prediction new data linear model
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: R: Predict method for Linear Model Fits

title: Formulas
text: A model formula has the outcome on the left of ~ and predictors on the right. y ~ . uses every other column, y ~ x1 * x2 adds an interaction, and categorical predictors (factors) are turned into indicator variables automatically.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Showing a fitted line with geom_smooth()
text: geom_smooth(method = "lm") adds a fitted straight line with a confidence band to a ggplot scatter plot; se = FALSE hides the band. It is for display only; use lm() to get the numbers.
keywords: regression line trend line geom_smooth fitted line
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Residuals and fitted values
text: residuals(model) gives the differences between observed and fitted values, and fitted(model) the predicted values for the training data. Plotting residuals against fitted values helps you spot curved patterns or uneven spread.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Training and test sets
text: To judge a model fairly, train it on one part of the data and test it on rows it has never seen. caret's createDataPartition(y, p = 0.7, list = FALSE) picks training rows while keeping the class balance similar in both parts. Set a seed first so the split is reproducible.
keywords: training set test set split data train test createDataPartition
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Support vector machines with kernlab::ksvm()
text: ksvm(label ~ ., data = train) from kernlab fits a support vector machine for classification when the outcome is a factor. kernel = "rbfdot" is the default; C sets the cost of misclassification and cross = adds k-fold cross validation.
keywords: support vector machine svm ksvm kernlab classification
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Support vector machines with e1071::svm()
text: svm(label ~ ., data = train) from e1071 is another SVM implementation. If the outcome is a factor it does classification; if numeric, regression. kernel and cost are the main settings to tune.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Decision trees with rpart()
text: rpart(label ~ ., data = train, method = "class") grows a classification tree that splits the data with simple yes or no rules. Trees are easy to explain; control settings such as cp limit how complex the tree gets.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: R: Recursive Partitioning and Regression Trees

title: Plotting trees with rpart.plot
text: The rpart.plot package draws an rpart tree with readable labels at each split: rpart.plot(tree). It is the easiest way to explain a tree model to a non-technical audience.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Predicting with a tree
text: predict(tree, newdata = test, type = "class") returns the predicted class for each test row; type = "prob" returns class probabilities instead.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: R: Predictions from a Fitted Rpart Object

title: Confusion matrix and accuracy
text: A confusion matrix cross-tabulates predicted against actual classes; table(predicted, actual) builds one. caret's confusionMatrix(predicted, actual) also reports accuracy, sensitivity and specificity. Both arguments should be factors with the same levels.
keywords: confusion matrix accuracy sensitivity specificity evaluate classifier
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Predicting with an SVM
text: predict(model, test) applies a fitted ksvm model to new rows and returns predicted classes; for ksvm, type = "probabilities" works when the model was fitted with prob.model = TRUE.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Association rules with apriori()
text: apriori(trans, parameter = list(supp = 0.01, conf = 0.5)) from the arules package finds rules like {bread} => {butter}. Support is how often the items appear together, confidence is how often the rule holds when the left side appears, and lift compares that with chance.
keywords: association rules apriori market basket support confidence lift
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: Mining Associations with the Apriori Algorithm | apriori • arules

title: Transactions objects
text: arules works on a transactions object, a sparse yes or no table of items per basket. Convert a list of baskets or a data frame of factors with as(x, "transactions"), and use itemFrequencyPlot() to see the most common items.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: Class transactions | Binary Incidence Matrix for Transactions | transactions-class • arules

title: Reading rules with inspect()
text: inspect(rules) prints rules in readable form with their support, confidence and lift. Sort first, for example inspect(head(sort(rules, by = "lift"), 10)), to see the strongest rules.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: Display Associations and Transactions in Readable Form | inspect • arules

title: Lift
text: Lift above 1 means the items appear together more often than if they were independent; lift near 1 means no real association. A rule with high confidence but lift near 1 may just reflect a very common right-hand item.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: Mining Associations with the Apriori Algorithm | apriori • arules

title: Structure of a Shiny app
syllabus_topic: Lecture 11: Interactive apps (Shiny) and deep learning
text: A Shiny app has a ui that defines the page and a server function(input, output) that computes the outputs. shinyApp(ui, server) puts them together and runs the app in a browser.
keywords: shiny app interactive web app ui server
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: Create a Shiny app object | shinyApp

title: Page layout with fluidPage()
syllabus_topic: Lecture 11: Interactive apps (Shiny) and deep learning
text: fluidPage() creates a page that resizes with the browser window. Put titlePanel(), sidebarLayout() and other elements inside it to arrange inputs and outputs.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: Create a page with fluid layout | fluidPage

title: Inputs such as sliderInput()
syllabus_topic: Lecture 11: Interactive apps (Shiny) and deep learning
text: sliderInput("n", "Sample size", min = 10, max = 500, value = 100) adds a slider. The first argument is the inputId; the server reads the current value as input$n.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Outputs: renderPlot() and plotOutput()
syllabus_topic: Lecture 11: Interactive apps (Shiny) and deep learning
text: In the server, output$hist <- renderPlot({ ... }) builds a plot; in the ui, plotOutput("hist") shows it. The ids must match. The plot re-runs automatically when any input it uses changes.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: reactive() expressions
syllabus_topic: Lecture 11: Interactive apps (Shiny) and deep learning
text: reactive({ ... }) turns a piece of code into a reactive expression: its value is worked out again whenever the inputs it reads change. Call it with parentheses, like data(), inside render functions. Use it to avoid repeating the same filtering in several outputs.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Deep learning from R with keras3
syllabus_topic: Lecture 11: Interactive apps (Shiny) and deep learning
text: The keras3 package is an R interface to Keras for building neural networks layer by layer. It runs on a Python backend that has to be installed, so it needs more setup than ordinary R packages.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Corpora with tm
syllabus_topic: Lecture 12: Text mining (word clouds and sentiment)
text: The tm package stores a collection of documents as a corpus, for example VCorpus(VectorSource(texts)). Cleaning steps are applied to every document with tm_map().
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Cleaning text with tm_map()
syllabus_topic: Lecture 12: Text mining (word clouds and sentiment)
text: tm_map(corpus, content_transformer(tolower)) lower-cases every document; other common steps are removePunctuation, removeNumbers, stripWhitespace and removeWords with stopwords("english").
keywords: clean text lowercase punctuation stopwords tm_map
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Term-document matrices
syllabus_topic: Lecture 12: Text mining (word clouds and sentiment)
text: TermDocumentMatrix(corpus) counts how often each word appears in each document (DocumentTermMatrix() is the same table turned around). Convert it with as.matrix() and sum the rows to get overall word frequencies.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Word clouds
syllabus_topic: Lecture 12: Text mining (word clouds and sentiment)
text: wordcloud(words, freq) from the wordcloud package draws more frequent words larger. min.freq drops rare words and max.words caps how many are shown. Set a seed first so the layout is the same each time.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: Tokenising with tidytext::unnest_tokens()
syllabus_topic: Lecture 12: Text mining (word clouds and sentiment)
text: unnest_tokens(df, word, text) splits a text column into one word per row, lower-cased with punctuation removed. You can then count words with dplyr and remove stop words with anti_join(stop_words).
keywords: tokenize tokenise words tidytext unnest_tokens text mining
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: Split a column into tokens | unnest_tokens • tidytext

title: Sentiment lexicons with get_sentiments()
syllabus_topic: Lecture 12: Text mining (word clouds and sentiment)
text: get_sentiments("bing") returns a table of words labelled positive or negative; "afinn" gives scores from -5 to 5 and "nrc" gives emotions. Join it to your tokens with inner_join() and count to measure sentiment. Some lexicons are downloaded on first use and have their own licences.
keywords: sentiment analysis sentiment lexicon positive negative
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: Get a tidy data frame of a single sentiment lexicon | get_sentiments • tidytext

title: quanteda tokens()
syllabus_topic: Lecture 12: Text mining (word clouds and sentiment)
text: The quanteda package is another text toolkit. tokens(texts, remove_punct = TRUE) splits texts into words, and tokens_remove(toks, stopwords("en")) drops common words.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: Construct a tokens object | tokens • quanteda

title: quanteda document-feature matrix
syllabus_topic: Lecture 12: Text mining (word clouds and sentiment)
text: dfm(tokens) builds a document-feature matrix: one row per document, one column per word, with counts. topfeatures(d) lists the most frequent words, and the matrix can feed a word cloud or a model.
keywords: quanteda dfm document feature matrix word frequency
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: Create a document-feature matrix | dfm • quanteda

title: "could not find function"
text: This error means R does not know the function name in this session: the package that provides it is not loaded, the name is misspelled, or it is your own function that has not been run yet. Load the package with library() or use pkg::function().
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: R: Loading/Attaching and Listing of Packages

title: "object not found"
text: "object 'x' not found" means no object with that name exists in this session: it was never created, it was created in another session, or the name is spelled differently (R is case sensitive). Run the line that creates it, then check with ls() or exists("x").
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: "non-numeric argument to binary operator"
text: This error appears when arithmetic such as + or * is used on text. Often a column that looks numeric was read as character. Check with class() or str() and convert with as.numeric() after removing symbols.
keywords: non-numeric argument to binary operator error
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: "unexpected symbol" and other syntax errors
text: "Error: unexpected symbol" means R could not parse the line: a missing comma, bracket or quote, or two names typed side by side. Look just before the position R reports, and check that brackets and quotes are balanced.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.

title: "subscript out of bounds"
text: This error means you asked for an element, row or column that does not exist, for example x[[5]] when the list has 4 elements or a misspelled column name in m[, "name"]. Check length(), dim() and names() first.
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
page_title: R: Extract or Replace Parts of an Object

title: "arguments imply differing number of rows"
text: data.frame() raises this when the vectors you combine have different lengths that cannot be recycled. Check length() of each vector before building the data frame.
keywords: arguments imply differing number of rows error data frame
written_by: Data360 team, in our own words
licence: Our own wording. The linked page keeps its own licence.
